descriptionChirho: To dig or excavate the ground, forming a pit, well, or grave. The primary and most frequent sense of the root, used in Qal active across many inflections (perfect, imperfect, participle, consecutive imperfect). Found in Genesis 26:25 (digging a well), Exodus 21:33 (digging a pit), Numbers 21:18 (digging a well with staves), 2 Chronicles 16:14, Psalms 7:15, 57:6, 119:85, Proverbs 16:27, 26:27, and Jeremiah 18:20,22. Multilingual glosses are uniform: Arabic حفر (dig), German gruben/dug, Hindi खोदा (dug), Korean 파다 (dig), Spanish cavar/excavar (dig/excavate).

The passive (Nifal) form of the root, meaning to be dug or to be excavated. Found only in Psalm 94:13, describing a pit being dug for the wicked. The Nifal stem marks a genuine morphological and semantic distinction from the active Qal. Glosses reflect passive voice: Hindi खोदी जाए (let it be dug), Korean 파여지리라 (will be dug), Spanish sea cavada (be dug).

A secondary meaning of the root used in commercial or transactional contexts: to bargain, negotiate, or trade. Found in Job 6:27 and Job 41:6(H), where the sense of 'digging' is metaphorically extended to haggling or trading. The multilingual glosses diverge noticeably from the literal digging sense: English 'bargain', Hindi खरीदेंगे (will buy), Spanish negociaran (will negotiate), while Korean maintains 파다 (dig) showing the metaphorical bridge.

A figurative extension of the root meaning to open or pierce, specifically used of God opening the ears in Psalm 40:7 (Hebrew 40:6). This is a well-known crux where כרה is applied metaphorically to ears (אזנים כרית לי, 'ears you have dug/opened for me'). Korean renders it 열어 주셨도다 (you opened), Arabic فتحت (you opened), Spanish abriste (you opened), all indicating the 'opening' rather than literal digging sense.
